comment.value:
This paper presents Face-Human-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating MLLMs on face and human-understanding tasks across a three-level taxonomy, covering both English and Chinese, with evaluations on 25 models. 

It received 3 Accept, 1 Borderline Accept, and 1 Borderline Reject ratings. Reviewers praise its breadth of tasks, detailed experimental design, insightful analyses, and novel metrics, recognizing its value as the dedicated benchmark in this space. Concerns were raised on limited sample size per sub-task, reliance on multiple-choice format, potential dataset biases, and some data presentation issues. The rebuttal clarified design choices, justified sample sizes with references to existing benchmarks, addressed bias analysis, and explained the “random” row values, which alleviated most concerns. 

Overall, given the strong contribution, comprehensive evaluation, and satisfactory rebuttal, the AC recommends acceptance, with the camera-ready to expand bias/fairness reporting, and acknowledge the limitation of multiple-choice-only evaluation with a plan for open-ended tasks in future work.

author_final_remarks.value:
Our work is among the first to investigate MLLMs in terms of face and human understanding comprehensively. Through systematic evaluation, we provide important reference values for researchers in the face and human community to conduct related studies using MLLMs. We provide sufficient details to enable readers to reproduce all our experiments (including a meticulously organized 35-page appendix). Future researchers can use our provided Face-Human-Bench dataset to evaluate newly developed MLLMs in face and human understanding.

The reviewers recognized several strengths of our work:
- The dataset setup is described as "comprehensive (v8on and qc4Z)", "novel (BNuf)", and "systematic and reproducible (dZWi)".
- The experiments are "extensive, easy to reproduce(v8on)", "sufficient and convincing (BNuf)",  "with a large number, rich content" (qc4Z), "well presented and informative (dZWi)".
- The writing is "clear and logically organized (v8on)", "easy to follow (BNuf)", and "well written (dZWi)".

After the rebuttal, the concerns of reviewers BNuf, qc4Z, and dZWi have been addressed, and they indicated a willingness to increase their scores or accept our paper. We also provided detailed explanations addressing seven issues raised by reviewer v8on, who has not yet responded.

rebuttal.value:
For Q1:
The objective of our study is to investigate the face and human understanding capabilities of MLLMs. Although the face and human communities have constructed datasets such as UCF-101, HumanVid, and Humman, which contain abundant information on faces and humans, the lack of annotated textual instructions prevents their direct utilization for evaluating MLLM capabilities. Currently, there is a lack of dedicated benchmarks specifically designed to assess the face and human understanding abilities of MLLMs. Existing benchmarks like MME, SEED-Bench, and MMBench, which primarily evaluate the general capabilities of MLLMs, include only a limited number of samples pertaining to face and human understanding.

---

For Q2:
In designing the questions, we adopted task definitions established within the face and human communities as our standard. These definitions represent the most widely recognized and critical tasks developed by these communities over the past decade.

While we acknowledge that the multiple-choice format may potentially restrict open-ended MLLMs' ability, our evaluation aims to effectively quantify MLLM performance while ensuring ease of assessment for subsequent researchers evaluating newly developed MLLMs. The multiple-choice format is currently the predominant evaluation paradigm for MLLMs. Introducing open-ended questions would necessitate either human evaluation or scoring systems based on LLMs. The former approach compromises evaluation consistency, while the latter requires subsequent researchers to either procure commercial API services or deploy local LLMs, both of which hinder straightforward and reliable reproducibility. We contend that, as the first comprehensive benchmark dedicated to evaluating MLLMs' face and human understanding capabilities, employing multiple-choice questions provides readers with substantial reference information while balancing evaluation costs. We plan to explore the incorporation of open-ended questions in future work to enable a more in-depth investigation of MLLM capabilities.

Our benchmark dataset comprises 3,600 samples (1,800 samples in the development set and 1,800 in the test set) separately for both Chinese and English versions. When determining the sample amount, we referenced highly cited works within the MLLM evaluation field. For instance, MMBench [1], aiming for a comprehensive assessment of diverse vision-language capabilities in MLLMs and also utilizing multiple-choice questions, contains 3,217 test samples, with the number per specific capability ranging between 125 and 246. In our dataset, the number of test samples per L2-level capability ranges from 100 to 250, representing a comparable scale. Given the substantial computational overhead associated with MLLM evaluation, an excessively large test sample size is impractical. The current sample size effectively balances testing cost and quality, meeting the assessment needs of both current and future researchers. Furthermore, the test results presented in Table 1 demonstrate that our dataset exhibits strong discriminative power across tasks.

[1] Liu, Yuan, et al. "Mmbench: Is your multi-modal model an all-around player?." European conference on computer vision. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland, 2024.

---

For Q3:
Our study presents the first comprehensive benchmark assessing the face and human understanding capabilities of current MLLMs. All evaluated tasks represent the most critical concerns within the face and human communities. By balancing testing cost and quality, we have substantially explored and demonstrated the perception abilities of MLLMs. We intend to investigate more nuanced and profound capabilities in future work.

In Table 3, we have compared the performance of MLLMs against feature-based models (indicated by the "Early Specialist Model" row) across the majority of L3 capabilities. Further experimental details can be found in Appendix B.3.

---

For Q4:
In Line 162, we note that "the 13B versions of LLaVA-1.5 and LLaVA-Next perform slightly worse than their 7B counterparts." We highlight this observation to underscore that the expected positive scaling of performance with model size—commonly observed in large models—does not always hold in our benchmark. We posit that this anomaly likely stems from the severely insufficient volume of face/human-focused instructional data in the training datasets for these models. This critical shortage prevented models with larger parameter counts from yielding their anticipated advantage in generalization.

Performance differentials between newer models and the earlier models arise from complex interacting factors, including architectural refinements, training procedure optimizations, enhanced loss function supervision, and improved training data quality.
What we can confirm is that newer models almost always use higher-quality training data (see the following Table, models are listed in order of release).

|Model|Data|
|---|---|
|LLaVA|558K filtered image-text pairs from LAION/CC/SBU, captioned by BLIP; 80K GPT-generated multimodal instruction-following data.|
|LLaVA-1.5|558K filtered image-text pairs from LAION/CC/SBU, captioned by BLIP; 158K GPT-generated multimodal instruction-following data; 450K academic-task-oriented VQA data mixture; 40K ShareGPT data.|
|LLaVA-NeXT|Pre-training Stage: LAION-GPT-V, ShareGPT-4V, DocVQA, SynDog-EN, ChartQA, DVQA, AI2D, RefCOCO/+/g, Toloka, LLaVA-150K, SVIT, VisDial, LRV-Instruction, LLaVA-Mix-665K Fine-tuning Stage: COCO Caption, TextCaps, VQAv2, OKVQA, A-OKVQA, IconQA, AI2D, GQA, OCR-VQA, ChartQA, DocVQA, ST-VQA, EST-VQA, InfoVQA, LLaVAR|
|InternVL-Chat-v1.2-Plus|LAION-en, LAION-COCO, COYO, SBU, CC3M, CC12M, Wukong, LAION-multi|
|InternVL-Chat-v1.5|Pre-training Stage: Laion-EN, Laion-ZH, COYO, GRIT, COCO, TextCaps, Objects, GRIT, All-Seeing, Wukong-OCR, LaionCOCO-OCR, Common Crawl PDF, MMC-Inst, LSVT, ST-VQA, RCTW-17, ReCTs, ArT, SynthDoG, COCO-Text, ChartQA, CTW, DocVQA, TextOCR, PlotQA, InfoVQA Fine-tuning Stage: TextCaps, ShareGPTV, VQAv2, GQA, OKVQA, VSR, VisualDialog, AID, ScienceQA, TQA, ChartQA, MMC-Inst, DVQA, PlotQA, LRV-Instruction, GeoQA+, TabMWP, MathQA, CLEVR-Math/Super, Geometry3K, KVQA, A-OKVQA, ViQuAE, Wikipedia, OCRVQA, InfoVQA, TextVQA, ArT, COCO-Text, CTW, LSVT, RCTW-17, ReCTs, SynthDoG, ST-VQA, DocVQA, Common Crawl PDF, RefCOCO/+/g, Visual Genome, LLaVA-150K, LVIS-Instruct4V, ALLaVA, Laion-GPT4V, TextOCR-GPTV, SVIT,OpenHermes2.5, Alpaca-GPT, ShareGPT, COIG-CQIA|


Moreover, the foundational LLMs and visual encoders used for each model are cataloged comprehensively in Table 14 (Appendix B.1) for reference.

---

For Q5:
In Section 3.3, several task pairs exhibited high correlations (r > 0.8). Given our evaluation across 25 MLLMs (n = 25), the positive correlations are statistically significant (t(23) ≈ 6.39, p < 0.001).

---

For Q6:
We first address the significant performance improvement observed in closed-source models when using hints and CoT instructions:
For closed-source models, applying hints clarifying task objectives triggers the utilization of pre-existing visual-language representations relevant to the specific knowledge, thereby enhancing performance. When incorporating CoT instructions, these models activate their step-by-step reasoning capabilities. This structured reasoning process generates accurate intermediate analyses, upon which the final prediction depends, ultimately yielding higher accuracy.

In stark contrast, open-source models exhibit minimal improvement under identical conditions:
Hints fail to activate enhanced visual comprehension in open-source models. With CoT prompting, these models struggle to produce valid analytical reasoning—often merely reiterating information from questions or options—rather than generating meaningful inference outputs. Consequently, their performance remains unaffected by these techniques.

This inability of open-source models to benefit from hints or CoT instructions stems from fundamental limitations in visual-language understanding and complex reasoning. We attribute this primarily to: 1) Scarcity of vision-language training samples aligned with evaluation tasks of face and human understanding. 2) Insufficient exposure to samples of the complex reasoning paradigm during training. 3) Inadequate model capacity due to substantially smaller parameter scales compared to closed-source MLLMs
Collectively, these constraints manifest as deficient generalization capability in open-source MLLMs.
We concur that "insufficient generalization" warrants further elaboration. We will expand on this analysis in the revised manuscript.

---

For Q7:
DeepFake Detection requires models to recognize subtle textural artifacts – technical traces left by manipulation techniques. However, existing MLLMs' training data predominantly focuses on image content understanding. These forensic artifacts lack effective alignment to language space.

Crowd Counting requires a model to first precisely localize human objects within an image, and subsequently map this visual information into the natural language space for reasoning-based counting. Current MLLMs face several significant limitations: 1) Architecturally, they lack inherent support for direct supervision of localization, making it difficult for the model to accurately localize all human objects within an image. 2) The LLMs used as the foundation for many MLLMs possess insufficient reasoning capabilities. 3) When LLMs are adapted into MLLMs, their reasoning capabilities further deteriorate due to the "alignment tax". These combined factors render current MLLMs sensitive to the Crowd Counting task.

For Q1: 
When determining the sample amount, we referenced highly cited works within the MLLM evaluation field. For instance, MMBench [1], aiming for a comprehensive assessment of diverse vision-language capabilities in MLLMs and also utilizing multiple-choice questions, contains 3,217 test samples, with the number per specific capability ranging between 125 and 246. In our dataset, the number of test samples per L2-level capability ranges from 100 to 250, representing a comparable scale. Given the substantial computational overhead associated with MLLM evaluation, an excessively large test sample size is impractical. The current sample size effectively balances testing cost and quality, meeting the assessment needs of both current and future researchers. Furthermore, the test results presented in Table 1 demonstrate that our dataset exhibits strong discriminative power across tasks.

[1] Liu, Yuan, et al. "Mmbench: Is your multi-modal model an all-around player?." European conference on computer vision. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland, 2024.

---

For Q2:
In Appendix A.3.2, we detail the option construction process for all 18 L3 tasks. In fact, only the incorrect options for the Action Recognition and Identity Reasoning tasks were generated entirely by GPT.
For Action Recognition, we designed prompts requiring the generated actions to modify only the verb while ensuring the resulting descriptions remained commonsensical. An example is provided in Table 9.
For Identity Reasoning, our prompts specified that the generated professions must be closely related to the correct answer and situated within a unified workplace setting. An example is provided in Table 10.
Furthermore, we implemented a manual check step to prevent the inclusion of low-quality options that were fundamentally implausible or violated commonsense understanding.

---

For Q3:
Precisely. The core objective of our study is to evaluate the face and human understanding capabilities of MLLMs. 
We hope future researchers can also use the data in our benchmarks to evaluate newly developed MLLMs. 
To guarantee the reliability of evaluations with this benchmark, the implementation of a manual check for all samples is essential.

---

For Q4:
Our work presents the first comprehensive evaluation specifically designed to assess the face and human body understanding capabilities of MLLMs. To reflect the current research landscape, we report results for numerous high-impact open-source MLLMs released since 2023, such as LLaVA, LLaVA-1.5, MiniGPT-4, and InstructBLIP, as these models are most frequently adopted as base architectures in existing studies.
This focus on widely-used models directly influenced our dataset construction strategy. We intentionally avoided exclusively selecting samples from highly challenging sources. This choice prevents the scenario where all evaluated models exhibit poor performance, which would result in metrics clustering within a very narrow numerical range. Instead, our approach facilitates effective differentiation of models operating at varying competency levels, thereby providing readers with more informative and actionable references.

Acknowledging the face community's emphasis on the face recognition robustness, our L3 incorporates five distinct scenarios for face recognition: Basic, Cross-Pose, Cross-Age, Similar-Looking, and Occluded. As evident from Table 1, all scenarios except Basic present significant challenges.

In our future study, we will introduce more difficult samples for tasks involving facial attribute Recognition, human attribute recognition, and social relationship understanding to maintain the benchmark challenging for future generations of MLLMs.

---

For Q5:
Our investigation into task performance correlations aims to determine whether improvements in one capability may transfer to others within MLLMs. For instance, Figure 3(c) suggests that significantly enhancing face recognition through additional training data would likely yield commensurate gains in human recognition, whereas face attack detection capabilities would remain largely unaffected. This analysis provides actionable insights for future researchers on optimizing training data to efficiently advance holistic face and human understanding in MLLMs.

Notwithstanding high inter-task correlations, each evaluated task represents a distinct capability with unique definitions and objectives; they should not be considered redundant. Furthermore, these tasks were not arbitrarily selected for our benchmark construction. Instead, they represent the most widely recognized and critical tasks developed by face/human communities over the past decade.

strengths_contributions.value:
1.The presentation is clear and logically organized.
2.The method and dataset proposed in this paper is comprehensive and supported by extensive experiments. The authors conduct extensive experiments to validate their benchmark.
3.The paper provides sufficient implementation details, making it easy to understand and reproduce.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1.In Line 33, as authors claimed that “existing benchmarks … involve limited abilities of face and human understanding, …”, I wonder what lead to such problem? Many datasets are collected from real word, movies, and stream-media platform, like UCF-101 [1], HumanVid [2], and Humman [3]. These videos also contain abundant faces and humans information, including identity, human action, and so on.
2.To construct the benchmark, the paper uses a semi-automatic data pipeline to obtain QA pairs. What’s the standard to design these questions? The multiple-choice format is also limited, which may restrict open-ended MLLMs ability and introduce bias, e.g., the model can guess the answer from given candidates. And my major concern is that the dev. and test set contain 1,800 questions across 18 abilities, separately. So, each ability only has 100 questions. If we divide these questions into English and Chinese, perception and reasoning, face and human, every sub-ability has too little data for evaluation. I think the conclusion of MLLMs maybe have obvious bias.
3.Based on the designed test set, authors evaluate 25 MLLMs and obtain some key insights. However, as I mention above, these insights are mainly come from multiple-choice QA pairs. It is hard to know whether one of the MLLMs has the real perception ability. Additionally, these results are not compared with feature-based action recognition, motion estimation, and emotion detection models and so on.
4.Thanks for the efforts in experiments, especially the Table 1. We can have an intuitive comparison with these models. However, the related analyses are limited. What I most interested is what lead to these different performances across these large models? Why 13B models perform worse than 7B counterparts? (Line 162) What make the differences between the newer models and the earlier models, the new model design, or the high-quality training data?
5.In Section 3.3, the higher correlation coefficient of face and human tasks can only demonstrate the model has the similar performance on the two tasks. We cannot infer that they have significant positive correlations.
6.In Section 3.5, authors find a good phenomenon that hints and CoT instructions cannot improve the performance of the open-source model. However, simply attribute this to the insufficient generalization capabilities of the open-source model is not convinced. Because open-source model also has the similar model structure and employ large amount of data for training. It is hard to say insufficient generalization.
7.In Section 3.6, why deepfake detection and crowd counting tasks are hard to be solved by MLLMs? I also wonder how makes these MLLM be sensitive to number counting task.

1. In Section 2.2, the paper says that the benchmark has a total of 1800 training samples and 1800 test samples. This is too few for the benchmark.
2. In Section 2.2, this paper proposes to use LLM (such as Chatgpt) to generate incorrect options. In this process, how to ensure that the quality of options generated by gpt is similar? For an incorrect option, sometimes gpt may generate very similar results that are difficult to distinguish, and sometimes it may generate very different results that are easy to distinguish. How to ensure consistency?
3. For the semi-supervised strategy proposed in this article, data reviewers are needed to ensure the uniqueness of the correct option. This step may be time-consuming.

However, the performance of many tasks is already very high (such as Attr. and Face Recognition in Face Understanding, or Attr. and Social Relation in Human Understanding), and many have an accuracy of 90%+ or even 95%+. This greatly reduces the significance of the benchmark research.
5. In Fig3, the author gives the correlation of different tasks, but lacks corresponding analysis, such as what problems in face and human understanding can this correlation analysis help solve. In addition, the correlation of many tasks is very high, does it indicate the redundancy of the benchmark?

Based on the author's response and other reviewer's review, it is sure that the contribution of the paper is significant. 

However, as I've pointed out, the data in the paper may be fabricated. Theoretically, the random method's accuracy is 25% or 50%, but actual experimental results are unlikely to be exactly 25.0 or 50.0. The presence of such data in the paper easily leads one to suspect fabrication. I acknowledge the paper's contributions and the authors' response, but this makes it difficult for me to give "accept" for a NeurIPS paper. I ultimately gave borderline accept simply because the contribution of the article outweighed this flaw. The author cannot just think that this is a small typo.

summary.value: This paper introduces Face-Human-Bench, a hierarchical benchmark designed to evaluate the facial and human understanding abilities of MLLMs. The benchmark is structured around a three-level ability taxonomy and includes 18 tasks, covering a range of comprehension levels from facial attributes and actions to complex reasoning involving social and spatial relationships. Using a semi-automatic data pipeline, the authors collect and annotate images from multiple datasets to create this comprehensive benchmark. Evaluations on 25 MLLMs reveal insights into model performance relative to task type, the impact of target object positioning, and the effectiveness of Chain-of-Thought  prompting. The results highlight areas where specialist models outperform MLLMs, emphasizing Face-Human-Bench's role as a holistic tool for assessing MLLM performance in understanding faces and humans.

strengths_contributions.value:
Strengths:

1.Face-Human-Bench is a comprehensive evaluation benchmark that covers a wide range of tasks relevant to facial and human understanding. It provides a holistic assessment of multimodal assistants' capabilities.

2.The paper evaluates 25 mainstream MLLMs, with a large number of experiments and rich content. This extensive experimental design provides a comprehensive basis for comparing model performance.

3.The paper introduces new metrics and evaluation protocols, such as RPSS for measuring sensitivity to the relative positioning of targets and percentile recall for assessing retrieval performance in large galleries. These new metrics provide more nuanced insights into model performance.

4.Face-Human-Bench supports both English and Chinese, which allows the benchmark to be used across language barriers.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1.While the benchmark covers diverse tasks, the paper could delve deeper into potential biases within the datasets, particularly regarding demographic representation in face and human recognition tasks.

2.Although Chain-of-Thought prompting is shown to improve closed-source models, its minimal impact on open-source models suggests limitations in its broader applicability.

3.There is confusion regarding the calculation of the overall score, specifically how weights for each sub-task are determined.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

final_justification.value: Overall, the authors' response has addressed all the key issues I raised. Therefore, I will maintain my original score of acceptance for this paper.

summary.value: This paper introduces Face-Human-Bench, a dedicated benchmark for evaluating multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) on face- and human-centric understanding. A three-level ability taxonomy underpins the benchmark. Results reveal large performance variance, indicating the dataset makes sense, and demonstrate strong positive correlations among several ability groups. Also substantial sensitivity to target position is included with experiments with sizable gains when hints + task-specific Chain-of-Thought prompting are used.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. While the topic of human and face evaluation is widely studied, the proposed benchmark still provides rigorous value by curating benchmark datasets and evaluation metrics in a systematic and reproducible way.
2. The paper is well written and easy to follow.
3. The visualizations are clear, interpretable, and all appear reasonable.
4. The rationale behind each section and the overall motivation are clearly presented and easy to understand.
5. The experimental details, along with illustrative examples, are well presented and informative.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. In Section 2.2, the benchmark's quadruple format includes an option set $O_i$, which implies a multiple-choice setting. It would be helpful to clarify whether the benchmark can also support open-ended questions, or whether it is strictly limited to multiple-choice formats.  
2. The issue of bias and fairness in human/face datasets is critically important. While the authors mention this briefly in Appendix D, I believe this aspect deserves more attention in the main body of the paper. In particular, additional benchmark results or analyses would help address the question of “which models perform best and most safely” from a fairness perspective.  
3. The evaluation metrics listed in Table 1 (e.g., DFD, FAS, RPU, CC, SRR, IR) are not explained or defined clearly. It would improve readability if the authors could briefly describe what each of these metrics stands for and why they are important for evaluation.  
4. Figure 3 has two specific issues:  
   - The color scale in the upper figures does not appear to reflect the actual values in the plots, which can cause confusion.  
   - It would be helpful to label the model names directly on the plot, or at least include a labeled version in the appendix. Since the figure aims to show which models perform well across both dimensions, this context is necessary—similar to what is done in Figure 2.  
5. A minor suggestion for discussion: In the calculation of RPSS, the authors use the summation of absolute values in Table 32. However, using root mean square might be another reasonable option, especially if the goal is to penalize larger deviations more heavily.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

final_justification.value: The authors have addressed most of the concerns raised in the initial review. One remaining limitation is the reliance on multiple-choice questions, but it does not significantly detract from the overall contribution of the paper. I recommend that the authors revise the future work section to explicitly acknowledge this limitation and suggest expanding to open-ended questions in future iterations.

title.value: Face-Human-Bench: A Comprehensive Benchmark of Face and Human Understanding for Multi-modal Assistants

abstract.value: Faces and humans are crucial elements in social interaction and are widely included in everyday photos and videos. Therefore, a deep understanding of faces and humans will enable multi-modal assistants to achieve improved response quality and broadened application scope. Currently, the multi-modal assistant community lacks a comprehensive and scientific evaluation of face and human understanding abilities. In this paper, we first propose a hierarchical ability taxonomy that includes three levels of abilities. Then, based on this taxonomy, we collect images and annotations from publicly available datasets in the face and human community and build a semi-automatic data pipeline to produce problems for the new benchmark. Finally, the obtained Face-Human-Bench includes a development set and a test set, each with 1800 problems, supporting both English and Chinese. We conduct evaluations over 25 mainstream multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) with our Face-Human-Bench, focusing on the correlation between abilities, the impact of the relative position of targets on performance, and the impact of Chain of Thought (CoT) prompting on performance. We also explore which abilities of MLLMs need to be supplemented by specialist models. The dataset and evaluation code have been made publicly available at https://face-human-bench.github.io.
